lesson.title: The Building Blocks of Matter
lesson.summary: This section introduces the basic structure of the atom, protons, neutrons, and electrons, and explains why the arrangement of electrons determines how atoms interact chemically, setting up everything else in biochemistry.
lesson.body:
Every living thing, from a bacterium to a redwood tree, is built from atoms, so understanding what an atom is and how it's put together is the starting point for all of biology's chemistry. An atom has a tiny, dense center called the nucleus, which holds two kinds of particles: protons, which carry a positive electrical charge, and neutrons, which carry no charge at all. Orbiting around this nucleus, but occupying a much larger volume of space, are electrons, which carry a negative charge. Because opposite charges attract, the negative electrons are held near the positive nucleus, and in an electrically neutral atom the number of electrons equals the number of protons, so the positive and negative charges balance out exactly.

The identity of an element is set by its number of protons, change that number and you have a different element entirely, but it's the electrons that determine how an atom behaves chemically, because electrons are what atoms actually use to interact with one another. Electrons don't swarm randomly around the nucleus; they occupy specific regions called energy levels, or shells, arranged in layers around the nucleus. The shell closest to the nucleus can hold at most 2 electrons; the next shell out can hold up to 8. Electrons fill the innermost available shell first, because being closer to the positively charged nucleus is a lower-energy, more stable arrangement. Only once an inner shell is full do additional electrons begin occupying the next shell out.

This filling pattern matters enormously because atoms are chemically "satisfied" when their outermost occupied shell is full, and unsatisfied when it isn't. An atom with a partially filled outer shell is reactive: it will tend to gain, lose, or share electrons with other atoms to reach a full outer shell, and this tendency is the root cause of chemical bonding. An atom whose outer shell is already full has little drive to react with anything, which is why some elements are chemically inert while others combine readily.

Carbon is the clearest example of why this matters for life. A carbon atom has 6 electrons total: 2 fill its inner shell, leaving 4 electrons in its outer shell. Since the outer shell of a low-numbered element like carbon needs 8 electrons to be full, carbon is 4 electrons short of stability. Rather than gaining or losing electrons outright, carbon achieves a full outer shell by sharing electrons with other atoms through covalent bonds, and because it needs exactly 4 more electrons, it forms exactly 4 covalent bonds at once. This capacity to form four simultaneous bonds, to other carbons, to hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen, and more, lets carbon build long chains, branches, and rings, which is precisely why carbon serves as the structural backbone of the organic molecules that make up living cells. Everything you'll learn next about molecules and bonds traces back to this simple fact about how electrons fill shells.
